metadata.title: Hits, misses and locality: does the loop fit in the cache?
metadata.subject: Computer Science
metadata.objective: Show why a cache hit is cheaper than a main-memory access and how locality decides how often the cache can answer.
metadata.learner: Knows basic computer organization: a processor, a cache and main memory.
misconceptions: The cache is faster for every access
A bigger cache is always better
expectedUnderstanding: Every access asks the cache first: a hit stops there and returns, while a miss must continue to main memory and bring the line back, so the miss path is the longer one.
The cache holds a fixed number of lines; a loop that touches more lines than the cache holds will have its lines evicted before they are reused.
Locality means the working set is small, so a tight loop fits and most accesses become hits after the first pass.
Capacity is a tradeoff, not a free win: once the cache covers the working set, more capacity buys nothing for this loop, and larger caches cost area and take longer to search.

primitives.text: Hits, misses and locality: does the loop fit in the cache?
blue: a hit is answered at the cache
red: a miss carries on to memory
Blue must reach past red for every loop line to stay resident. Short of that, reuse finds the line gone, and a cache does not shorten a miss.

controls.label: how many lines the loop touches
how many lines the cache holds

checkpoints.title: Predict from the bars
checkpoints.body: The red bar is longer than the blue. In one sentence, what does that predict about the accesses the loop makes on its second pass, and which level answers them?

checkpoints.title: The bars meet
checkpoints.body: Blue has just reached red. What is true now that was not true at two lines, and what is still true about the loop's very first pass?

checkpoints.title: Past the red bar
checkpoints.body: The blue bar is now well past the red. What did the extra capacity buy for this loop, and what does a larger cache cost you?

checkpoints.title: The gap returns
checkpoints.body: Capacity has fallen below the loop size and the loop is growing. Why is a line evicted before it is reused, and does the cache make that access any faster than going straight to memory?

narration.text: Three levels: the processor, a small cache, and main memory. Every access asks the cache first. A hit is answered there and comes back; a miss has to carry on to memory and bring the line back, which is the longer trip.
The red bar is how many lines the loop touches on each pass. The blue bar is how many lines the cache can hold. The comparison between those two bars decides almost everything.
While the blue bar is short of the red, some of the loop's lines are pushed out before the loop comes back to them, so those accesses miss and pay the memory trip.
When blue reaches red, every line the loop uses can stay resident, and after the first pass the repeats are hits. Equal is enough: the bars have to meet, not one dominate.
Capacity past the red bar buys nothing for this loop, and a bigger cache costs area and takes longer to search. More capacity is a tradeoff, not an automatic improvement.
Shrink the cache and widen the loop, and the gap comes back. The lines no longer fit, reuse finds them gone, and those accesses pay the trip to memory again.

fallback.text: A hierarchy diagram on the left: a CPU box at the top, a CACHE box in the middle outlined in blue, and a MAIN MEMORY box at the bottom, with a short blue arrow from the CPU to the cache labelled as a hit and a red arrow from the cache to memory labelled as the extra leg a miss must travel. On the right, two horizontal bars share a left origin: a red bar showing how many lines the loop touches, and a blue bar showing how many lines the cache holds. With the loop touching five lines and the cache holding two, the red bar is more than twice the blue, so loop lines are evicted before reuse. As capacity is raised to five the blue bar exactly meets the red, which is the point where all the loop's lines can stay resident and repeats hit; capacity raised to eight overshoots the red bar without further benefit, and capacity lowered to three leaves the red bar longer again.

accessibility.alt: A three level memory hierarchy drawn as stacked boxes: the CPU at the top, a cache below it outlined in blue, and main memory at the bottom. A short blue arrow joins the CPU to the cache, labelled as the hit path answered at the cache; a red arrow continues from the cache to main memory, labelled as the extra leg travelled on a miss, so the miss path is visibly the longer one. Beside the diagram, two horizontal bars start from a common left edge: a red bar for the number of lines the loop touches and a blue bar for the number of lines the cache holds. Two sliders change those numbers. When the blue bar falls short of the red bar, some loop lines cannot stay in the cache and their accesses miss; when blue reaches red, the working set fits and repeats hit; growth beyond the red bar shows that extra capacity does not help this loop.
